title: Component API design

sources.locator: React Learn and Reference; React 19.2; provisions applicable to Component API design
sources.claim: A component interface defines required and optional props, callbacks, controlled values, defaults, and semantic constraints.

canonicalExplanation.summary: A component's props are its **public interface**, like a function signature. A good interface is **small**: **required** props that it can't work without, a few **optional** props with **documented defaults**, **callbacks** named `onSomething`, and **constraints** it enforces itself, such as rendering a real `<button>` so keyboard and screen readers work. Prefer a `variant` prop with a few allowed values over five booleans that can conflict. Types, from TypeScript or JSDoc, catch wrong prop shapes, but they **can't guarantee** accessible or semantic behaviour; the component must build that in and tests must check it.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
The app's Button takes 14 props: `isPrimary`, `isDanger`, `isSmall`, `isLink`, `clickHandler`, `onClick`, `label`, `text`... Two teams pass different ones, some combinations look broken, and one version renders a div that keyboard users can't reach. A Button requires children and onPress while variant has a documented default and disabled behavior. In this lesson you'll review and simplify a component interface while documenting its contract.

What should the Button look like?", "options": ["Whatever CSS wins", "Nobody knows, which is why one `variant` prop with allowed values is better"], "answer": 1, "why": "Booleans that can conflict make impossible states possible. A single variant makes them impossible."}

examples.title: A Button with a clear contract
examples.situation: A Button requires children and onPress while variant has a documented default and disabled behavior.
walkthrough: **Review:** 14 props collapse into children, onPress, variant and disabled; conflicting booleans become one variant.
**Documented default:** variant defaults to "secondary", and disabled buttons can't be pressed.
**Check the contract:** a test will render Button, find it by role and name, press it with Enter, and confirm onPress runs once.
examples.result: Every team uses the same four props, impossible style combinations are gone, and keyboard users can always press it.

examples.title: The icon button nobody could name
examples.situation: A close button shows only an X icon. Screen-reader users hear "button" and can't tell what it does.
walkthrough: The interface allowed an icon without any text.
Make `label` a required prop for IconButton.
Render it as `aria-label={label}` and add a test that finds the button by that name.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: TypeScript prop types automatically guarantee the component is accessible and semantically valid.
misconceptions.correction: Types check the shape of props, not behaviour. Accessibility comes from the component's own markup (real buttons, labels, roles) and should be verified with tests.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The icon button nobody could name", what did the types allow?

analogy.example: A props interface is like **the controls on a microwave**: a couple of buttons you must use (start, time), a few with sensible defaults (power level), and built-in safety (it won't run with the door open). Fourteen unlabelled buttons that can fight each other would make it unusable.
limitations: Microwaves come with manuals; document your props too.
A label printed on a button is like aria-label for icon buttons.

farTransfer.prompt: Pick a component from your app, list how it's used across the codebase, then redesign its props, update the call sites, and add tests for required props, defaults and keyboard behaviour.

remediation.explanation: Write the component's contract in three lines: **required props, optional props with defaults, and what it guarantees** (semantics, keyboard, disabled). Anything that doesn't fit is a candidate to remove.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The icon button nobody could name".

recap.summary: To review and simplify a component interface, keep a small set of required props, a few optional ones with documented defaults, onSomething callbacks, and built-in constraints like native semantics. Replace conflicting booleans with one enumerated prop, and remember types don't guarantee accessibility; tests do.
